heading: An independent kingdom until 1949
body: For most of its history, Manipur was not part of any Indian state's story — it was its own kingdom. The Meitei kingdom of Kangleipak, centred on the Imphal valley, traces its own royal chronicle, the Cheitharol Kumbaba, back to the early centuries CE, and it was ruled continuously by the Ningthouja dynasty through a long, largely self-contained history quite distinct from developments on the subcontinent's plains. That independence ended in stages: the Anglo-Manipur War of 1891 brought the kingdom under British paramountcy as a princely state, though it retained its own ruler and internal administration in the manner typical of princely India.

Manipur's merger into independent India was more contested than most. In September 1949, the Maharaja signed an Instrument of Merger with the government of India, and a Chief Commissioner took over the state's administration from October 1949 — but the agreement was concluded without consulting Manipur's own elected legislative assembly, which had been functioning under a constitution adopted in 1947. That omission is still cited today, particularly by Meitei nationalist movements, as evidence that the merger was carried out under duress rather than through the state's own democratic institutions — a genuinely disputed point in the region's modern political history, not a settled one.

In between kingdom and merger, Manipur was thrust into a war it had no part in choosing. In 1944, the Japanese army's Operation U-Go tried to break through British lines at Imphal and Kohima to open a route into India; the resulting Battle of Imphal (March–July 1944) became one of the largest defeats in Japanese military history, with roughly 30,000 of 65,000 Japanese frontline troops killed, and is often called, alongside Kohima, the turning point of the entire Burma campaign. Manipur, a quiet corner of British India with few outside links before 1942, became one of the most fought-over pieces of ground in the whole war. The places on this map draw on both threads: the long, independent life of the Kangleipak kingdom, and the war that briefly made this valley one of the most consequential battlefields on earth.

sources.title: Manipur and Tripura: From Princely States to Modern Indian States
